q: 12 workers, working 8 hours a day, finish a job in 10 days. Which of the following teams, made of workers of the same efficiency, would finish the same job in at most 10 days?
solution:
The job needs $12\times8\times10=960$ worker-hours, i.e. at least 96 worker-hours per day for 10 days.
A: 96 → exactly 10 days ✓. B: 90 → $10\frac23$ days ✗.
C: 105 → about 9.1 days ✓. D: 88 → about 10.9 days ✗.
Answer: A, C.
verify:
from fractions import Fraction as F
need = 12 * 8 * 10
teams = [(16, 6), (10, 9), (15, 7), (8, 11)]
ans = [L for L, (w, h) in zip('ABCD', teams) if F(need, w * h) <= 10]

q:
The stacked bar chart shows the sales (in ₹ crore) of a company in its North, South and East regions from 2021 to 2024.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?
options: North's share of the total sales was at least 40% in exactly two of the four years.
East's sales grew by 20% from 2021 to 2024.
South's sales more than doubled from 2021 to 2023.
In every year, North had strictly higher sales than each of the other two regions.
solution:
(A) North's share: 40%, 41.7%, 33.3%, 37.5% → exactly two years (2021, 2022) ✓.
(B) East: $\frac{50-40}{40}=25\%$, not 20% ✗ (20% divides by 50).
(C) South: 20 → 45, more than $2\times20$ ✓.
(D) In 2021 North ties with East (40 each), and in 2023 all three are equal (45), so North was not strictly higher ✗.
verify:
N=[40,50,45,60]
S=[20,30,45,50]
E=[40,40,45,50]
T=[a+b+c for a,b,c in zip(N,S,E)]
from fractions import Fraction as F
A=sum(1 for n,t in zip(N,T) if F(n,t)>=F(2,5))==2
B=F(E[3]-E[0],E[0])==F(1,5)
Cc=S[2]>2*S[0]
D=all(N[i]>S[i] and N[i]>E[i] for i in range(4))
ans=[L for L,b in zip('ABCD',[A,B,Cc,D]) if b]

q: Three views of the same die, whose faces are numbered 1 to 6, are shown in the figure. Which number is on the face opposite to 2?
solution:
Faces seen next to 1: 2, 3 (view i), 4, 6 (view ii) ⇒ 1 is opposite 5.
Faces seen next to 6: 4, 1 (view ii), 5, 3 (view iii) ⇒ 6 is opposite the only face left, 2.
So 2 is opposite 6 (and 3 is opposite 4).
Trap: 5 is never seen with 2, but 5 is already opposite 1.

q: Three views of the same die, whose faces are numbered 1 to 6, are shown in the figure. In each view the top face, the front-left face and the front-right face are visible. If the die is placed with 4 on the top face and 5 on the front-left face, which number will be on the front-right face?
solution:
Opposite pairs: 1 is seen with 2, 3, 4, 6 ⇒ 1–5; 6 is seen with 1, 3, 4, 5 ⇒ 6–2; hence 3–4.
Hold the die as in view (ii): 4 up, 6 front-left, 1 front-right. Then 3 is down, 2 (opposite 6) is at the back-right and 5 (opposite 1) at the back-left.
Keep 4 on top and turn the die about the vertical axis so that 5 comes to the front-left: each side face moves one place, back-left → front-left, front-left → front-right. So 6 moves to the front-right.
Answer: 6.
Trap: 2 also touches both 4 and 5; it is the answer for the mirror-image die.

q: Three views of a die, whose faces are numbered 1 to 6, are shown in the first figure. Which one of the sheets shown in the options can be folded (numbers on the outside) to make this die?
solution:
From the views: 1 is seen with 2, 3, 4, 6 ⇒ 1–5; 6 is seen with 1, 3, 4, 5 ⇒ 6–2; so 3–4.
In each cross-shaped sheet the row of four gives the pairs (1st, 3rd) and (2nd, 4th), and the squares above and below the row are opposite.
C pairs 2–3 and 4–6: wrong. D pairs 2–6 and 1–3: wrong. A and B both give 1–5, 2–6, 3–4, so handedness decides.
Fold B with 4 in front: 1 top, 5 bottom, 2 left, 6 right, 3 back. Tip it backwards so 4 comes on top (1 goes to the back, 5 to the front), then give it a quarter turn so that 6 is at the front-left: 1 is then at the front-right — exactly view (ii).
Sheet A (1 and 5 exchanged) puts 5 at the front-right instead: it is the mirror image. Answer: B.
Trap: checking only opposite pairs leaves both A and B.
